title: The whole country, in plain English
deck: Six points from the national ledger, with the three verifiers' corrections and the red team's rulings applied. Every number links to the section that proves it, and every figure carries its grade and source.

points.title: Against the last midterm, the party mix barely moved
points.caption: of early ballots cast by registered Democrats ten days out in the 22 states that report by party, the same share as 2022; the bigger swings in the headlines measure against 2024
points.sentence: Same states, same day: Democrats cast 45.3% of early ballots, exactly their 2022 share, and Republicans 30.6% against 33.1%, so the 2.5-point move toward Democrats (1.0 to 2.7 allowing one day of misalignment) is fewer Republican ballots, not more Democratic ones. Neither year is a clean baseline (Republicans are being urged to vote early this year, and some states changed their early-vote rules since 2022), and party counts say who voted, not how.

points.title: More early ballots is not more voters
points.caption: early ballots nationwide (the Election Lab's state files, summed) against the same day of 2022 (26.55 million against 20.44 million, 10 days out)
points.sentence: The early vote is 30% above 2022 at the same point, but early ballots grew from about 33% of the final vote in 2018 to 41% in 2022 and 56% in 2024, so a bigger early vote is a change in habit (and, in some states, in the law) before it is a change in turnout.

points.title: The state that tests the theory best: Iowa
points.caption: Iowa early ballots by party registration, 11 days out; D+23.8 at the same point in 2022
points.sentence: Against the last midterm Iowa's early vote is about 5 points less Democratic (D+23.8 in 2022, D+18.9 now), and its polls were too Democratic in all eight statewide races since 2016.

points.title: The Senate leans Democratic, narrowly
points.caption: Democratic and independent Senate seats the Kalshi prices imply (34 not up, plus the summed prices of the 35 races); a 50-50 Senate is Republican control, because the vice president breaks ties, so Democrats need 51
points.sentence: The markets give Democrats a 64.5% to 66.5% chance of the Senate and Silver's model 76.4%, but our stress test, a repeat of the 4.1-point miss Senate polls showed in Trump-won states from 2018 to 2024, keeps it Republican 52 to 48.

points.title: The House leans Democratic every way we count it
points.caption: House seats leaning Democratic before toss-ups, across five methods (polls, adjusted polls, two historical misses, markets); 218 is control
points.sentence: Democrats lead under every method we ran, with 217 to 235 seats leaning their way before toss-ups, and the markets give them a 90.4% to 91.5% chance of control; Republicans hold the House only with a presidential-year-sized polling miss in the closest seats.
